pedagogy.summary: At age 10-11 children calculate the mean (add the values, divide by how many) AND interpret what it represents: the fair-share or typical value if the total were shared equally among the data points. The pedagogy's whole battle is against learning the rule as an empty procedure. A child who knows only 'add up and divide' makes predictable errors the moment a problem is not transparent — they cannot find a missing value given the mean, they believe adding a score of 0 leaves the mean unchanged, and they cannot say what the mean tells them or accept that it need not equal any actual data value. So the mean should be built as LEVELLING/FAIR SHARE (physically evening out towers of cubes to a common height) before or alongside the algorithm, and taught with the two 'non-transparent' tasks that reveal understanding: the reverse problem (find the missing value from the mean, using total = mean × count) and reasoning about how adding a value shifts the mean.
bestPractices: Build the mean as LEVELLING/FAIR SHARE first — even out unequal towers of cubes to a common height — so the algorithm is seen as sharing the total equally, not just a rule
Always ask 'what does this mean value tell us about the data?' after computing, and accept/expect that the mean need not equal any actual value (nobody scored 82, yet 82 is the mean)
Teach the mean as total = mean × count, so the reverse problem (find a missing value given the mean) is accessible — this is the task that reveals conceptual, not just procedural, knowledge
Probe the effect of changing the data: adding a 0, or an extreme value, MUST change the mean because it is influenced by every value — confront the common belief that a 0 leaves it unchanged
Connect the mean to its properties (it lies between the lowest and highest values; it balances the data) so children can sanity-check an answer that falls outside the data range
Keep the arithmetic (decimal addition and division) reliable so procedural slips don't masquerade as conceptual gaps
keyRepresentations: Towers of cubes / bars levelled to a common height (the fair-share / levelling model of the mean)
A balance-point image on a number line (the mean as the balancing value of the data)
The relationship triangle total = mean × count, used forwards (find mean) and backwards (find a missing value)
A data set with its mean marked, shown falling between the lowest and highest values but equal to none of them
commonMisconceptions: Knowing only the add-and-divide rule with no sense of what the mean represents, so any non-standard problem fails
Believing that adding a data value of 0 does not change the mean (not seeing that the mean is influenced by every value and that the count also rises)
Being unable to find a missing value given the mean — re-averaging the known values instead of using total = mean × count
Expecting the mean to equal one of the data values, or placing it outside the range of the data
Dividing by the wrong count (e.g. ignoring a zero or a repeated value when counting the data points)

learn.summary: Teach 10-11 year olds to calculate the mean (add the values, divide by the count) AND interpret it as the fair-share/levelling value: what each data point would be if the total were shared equally. The central aim is to prevent the mean becoming an empty procedure. Build it as levelling/fair share (evening out towers of cubes to a common height) alongside the algorithm, then use two revealing non-transparent tasks — the reverse problem (find a missing value using total = mean \u00d7 count) and reasoning about how adding a value (including 0) shifts the mean. Reinforce the properties that let children sanity-check: the mean lies between the lowest and highest values, is influenced by every value, and need not equal any actual data value.

activities.title: Level the towers: the mean as fair share
feedback: If a child only restates 'you add them and divide' when asked what the mean tells us, point back to the levelled towers: 'if everyone scored the same, this is the score each would get.'
Mirror the algorithm (sum \u00f7 count) next to the levelled towers so the child sees the two give the same number.
Optional interactive version: let the child drag cubes between towers and watch a read-out show the running mean; a 'balance beam' number line can show the mean as the balancing point of the data.
activities.rationale: Grounding the algorithm in levelling/fair share gives the mean a meaning children can reason from, addressing the misconception of knowing only the bare rule.
sourceClaims: The mean is productively taught as 'fair share' / levelling — evening out the data so each shares the total equally — which grounds the algorithm in a meaning

Knowing the computational rule for the mean does not imply understanding; students with only computational knowledge make predictable errors on all but the most transparent problems, and some believe that adding a value of 0 does not change the mean (though the mean is influenced by every value)
learnerActions: Start with five towers of cubes at different heights (e.g. representing scores), choosing heights whose total is a multiple of 5 so whole cubes can be shared equally, and even them out by moving cubes from the tall towers onto the short ones until every tower is the same height.
State that this common height IS the mean — what each would be if the total were shared equally.
Compute sum \u00f7 count and confirm it equals the levelled height, so the fair-share meaning and the rule are seen as the same thing.
Answer 'if all five pupils had scored the same, what would each have scored?' and 'what does this mean value tell us about the scores?'
activities.intendedInsight: The mean is the value every data point would share if the total were distributed equally; the add-and-divide algorithm computes exactly this fair share, so the rule has a meaning rather than being an arbitrary procedure.

activities.title: The reverse problem: find the missing value
feedback: If the child adds 7+9+6+10 and divides by 4, or divides by 5, point out they have ignored that the mean already describes five scores: ask 'what must all five add up to if their mean is 8?'
Optional interactive version: fix the mean line, hide one tower's height, and let the child drag it up and down until the row levels — discovering the total is fixed at mean \u00d7 count.
Confirm success when the child computes the total first (8\u00d75=40) then subtracts the known 32 to get 8.
activities.rationale: The reverse problem cannot be solved by the add-and-divide rule alone, so it reveals whether a child owns the fair-share meaning rather than just a procedure.
sourceClaims: Knowing the computational rule for the mean does not imply understanding; students with only computational knowledge make predictable errors on all but the most transparent problems, and some believe that adding a value of 0 does not change the mean (though the mean is influenced by every value)
The mean is productively taught as 'fair share' / levelling — evening out the data so each shares the total equally — which grounds the algorithm in a meaning
learnerActions: Given a mean and all-but-one of the values (e.g. four of five spelling scores were 7, 9, 6 and 10; the mean of all five is 8), find the missing value.
Reconstruct the total using total = mean \u00d7 count (8 \u00d7 5 = 40), subtract the known values (40 \u2212 32 = 8) to recover the missing one.
Explain why re-averaging only the known four values is wrong — the mean refers to all five.
activities.intendedInsight: Because the mean is the total shared equally, the total is fixed at mean \u00d7 count; recovering a missing value means finding that total and subtracting what is known, not re-averaging the visible data.

activities.title: Does a zero change the mean?
feedback: If the child says 'you're only adding a zero so it stays the same', recompute with and without the 0 and highlight both that the 0 sits below the current (positive) mean and that the count changed too, so the mean falls.
Optional interactive version: an 'add a new pupil who scored 0' button so the mean visibly shifts and the count updates as the child predicts then watches.
Reinforce that the mean is influenced by every value, so adding a value above the current mean (like 100) moves it up while a value below it (like 0 here) moves it down.
activities.rationale: Directly confronts the documented belief that adding a 0 leaves the mean unchanged, by having the child predict and then recompute on a concrete positive-score case.
sourceClaims: Knowing the computational rule for the mean does not imply understanding; students with only computational knowledge make predictable errors on all but the most transparent problems, and some believe that adding a value of 0 does not change the mean (though the mean is influenced by every value)

Strauss & Bichler's conceptual properties of the average include: it lies between the extreme values, it is influenced by every value, it need not equal one of the values, and it can be a fraction with no physical counterpart — properties children find harder than the bare procedure
learnerActions: Start from a stated data set of positive test scores with a known mean (e.g. 72, 85, 90, 68, 95 with mean 82), predict what happens to the mean when a new value of 0 is added, then recompute to check.
Notice that both the total and the count change (here from 5 values to 6), and that the new 0 still counts as a data point.

State that, because the existing scores are positive, the current mean is positive, so the added 0 lies below it: the mean goes DOWN (e.g. 410 \u00f7 6 \u2248 68.3), pulled toward zero as part of the fair share.
Extend to an extreme value: predict then compute the effect of adding one more score of 100 to the stated set (which, being above the current mean, pulls the mean up).
activities.intendedInsight: Every value — including 0 — influences the mean, and adding a data point also increases the count; for positive scores an added 0 sits below the current mean and lowers it, so it does not leave the mean unchanged.

activities.title: Properties of the mean: sanity-checking an answer
feedback: If a child expects the mean to match one of the scores, show a clear example where it does not and tie it back to fair share.
If a child produces a mean outside the data range, prompt: 'can a fair share be bigger than the biggest value?'

Optional reference: tapping a data set to reveal its total, count and mean, with a note that the mean equals none of the values, can serve as a static check — though it cannot let the child test how a new value moves the mean.
activities.rationale: Knowing the properties lets children detect errors and accept that the mean need not equal a data value, which is harder than the bare procedure.
sourceClaims: Strauss & Bichler's conceptual properties of the average include: it lies between the extreme values, it is influenced by every value, it need not equal one of the values, and it can be a fraction with no physical counterpart — properties children find harder than the bare procedure
learnerActions: For a data set with its mean marked, confirm the mean lies between the lowest and highest values and check it is not greater than every score nor less than every score.
Point out a case where the mean equals none of the actual values (e.g. nobody scored 82, yet 82 is the mean) and explain why that is fine.
Given a computed mean, judge whether it is plausible by checking it falls within the data range.
Answer the counterexample 'could the mean ever be higher than every single score? Why or why not?'
activities.intendedInsight: The mean always lies between the lowest and highest values (inclusive) and need not equal any actual data value (it can even be a fraction with no physical counterpart), so a mean outside the data range signals a computation error.

activities.title: Scorable practice and self-check
feedback: For the zero item, confirm 'down' for the positive-score set and explain the 0 sits below the current mean and the count rises; correct 'stays the same' by recomputing.
For the reverse item, confirm success only when the child uses the total (mean \u00d7 count), not re-averaging.
Keep data sets small and the arithmetic clean so a wrong answer reflects reasoning, not a calculation slip.
activities.rationale: Recognition and short-answer items give a scorable check that targets the specific misconceptions, though they verify less than independent construction and reasoning.
learnerActions: Compute the mean of a small clean data set (fill-in-the-blank).
Solve a reverse item: 'four of five scores are…; the mean is 8; find the fifth.'
Answer a multiple-choice item: 'a new pupil scores 0 — does the mean go up, down, or stay the same?' (for a set of positive scores).
Spot an implausible mean: choose which proposed mean cannot be right because it falls outside the data range.
activities.intendedInsight: Calculating, interpreting, reversing and sanity-checking the mean can each be checked against a correct answer, catching the zero and missing-value errors.

constraints: The levelling/fair-share model and the algorithm must be presented as the same thing, not as two separate topics; always ask what the mean value tells us after computing.

A static annotated data set can label the mean and show it between the extremes, but it cannot let the child level the data or test how a new value moves the mean; use it as reference only, not as the main builder.
Quiz/recognition items give a scorable check but do not elicit independent construction or explanation; pair them with tasks where the child computes, reverses and explains in their own words.
Keep decimal addition and division reliable so procedural slips are not mistaken for conceptual gaps; have the child count the data points first and recheck the arithmetic.
An interactive levelling model is one good way to make the fair-share idea concrete, but cube towers and a number line on paper can carry the same meaning; do not treat any one medium as required.

State direction-of-change predictions against the stated data: for positive scores an added 0 lowers the mean and a value above the current mean raises it; do not present a direction as a rule detached from the data set.
The mean of a one-dimensional data set does not use a third spatial dimension, so a 3D representation adds nothing for this particular content.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic self-audit: 72+85+90+68+95 = 410, 410\u00f75 = 82 (correct). Reverse example: 7+9+6+10 = 32; mean 8 \u00d7 5 = 40; 40\u221232 = 8 (correct). Adding a 0 to the five values (mean 82) gives total 410 over 6 = ~68.3, so the mean falls (consistent with 'down' for positive scores).
The 'adding a 0 lowers the mean' claim is conditioned on positive scores (so the current mean is positive); it is not stated as an unconditional rule for arbitrary data.

The Year 6 statutory curriculum claim establishes only topic and age-appropriateness; it was not cited as support for any specific teaching principle, so it was removed from activity sourceClaims where it only matched the topic.

The legacy framing that an in-role dialogue 'adds no verification' and that a static image 'cannot teach the core of understanding' was softened: these media offer different affordances and limits rather than being universally incapable.

Optional interactive features (drag cubes, balance-beam number line, hide-a-tower reverse mode, add-a-0 button) are presented as examples that make the mechanism concrete, not as mandatory mechanisms.

probeDeeper: 'Your mean is 82 but nobody actually scored 82 — how can that be?' — probes that the mean need not equal a data value
'If all five pupils had scored the same, what would each have scored?' — surfaces the fair-share meaning
Counterexample: 'Could the mean ever be higher than every single score? Why or why not?' — tests the between-the-extremes property
'What happens to the mean if I add one more score of 100? Predict, then work it out.' — checks that every value influences the mean, on a fresh case
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: for (1) sums to 410 and divides by 5 to get 82, and describes 82 as a typical / fair-share score that need not equal any actual score; for (2) uses total = mean × count (8×5 = 40), subtracts the known 32, giving 8 — not re-averaging the four; for (3) recomputes and states the mean goes DOWN because the 0 counts and pulls it toward zero (the count also rises). Solving the reverse problem and reasoning correctly about the zero are the marks of conceptual mastery.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mean as bare rule: computes add-and-divide but cannot say what the mean represents, treating it as just the answer to a calculation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach meaning via the vocabulary/fair-share prerequisite: level cube towers to a common height and ask 'if everyone scored the same, what would each score be?' so the mean carries a meaning, not just a rule
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (1) the child gets 82 but, asked what it tells us, restates 'you add them and divide' rather than describing a typical / fair-share score

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot reverse: given the mean and all-but-one values, re-averages the known values or divides by the wrong count instead of using total = mean × count
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the mean as the total shared equally: establish total = mean × count on a levelling model, then subtract the known values to recover the missing one
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (2) the child adds 7+9+6+10 and divides by 4 (getting 8) or by 5, rather than computing the total (8×5=40) and subtracting 32 to get 8

errorPatterns.pattern: Zero doesn't count: believes adding a data value of 0 leaves the mean unchanged, not seeing that the mean is influenced by every value and that the count rises too
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront by recomputing with and without the 0 (and note the count changed from 5 to 6); every value, including 0, is part of the fair share
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (3) the child says the mean stays the same because 'you're only adding a zero', rather than recomputing to see it fall

errorPatterns.pattern: Arithmetic slip: uses the right method but makes a decimal addition or division error, or miscounts the data points, giving a wrong mean
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: have the child count the data points first and recheck the addition/division; the concept is intact, only the calculation slipped
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The method is sound (sum then divide by the correct count) but the total or the quotient is wrong

responseLevels.gap: Applies add-and-divide unreliably (divides by the wrong count) or not at all; treats the mean as a real data value and thinks adding a 0 leaves it unchanged
responseLevels.full: Computes the mean, interprets it as the fair-share / typical value that lies between the extremes and need not equal any score, solves the reverse problem via total = mean × count, and reasons correctly that adding a value (including 0) shifts it — transferring to a fresh data set
responseLevels.partial: Computes the mean of a plain list correctly and names it the average, but cannot solve the reverse missing-value problem and cannot explain what the mean represents or that it need not equal an actual value — has the rule, not the fair-share meaning

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set these tasks and WATCH how the child works, saying little. (1) 'Here are five test scores: 72, 85, 90, 68, 95. Work out the mean, and tell me what that number tells us about the scores.' (2) A reverse task: 'Four of five spelling scores were 7, 9, 6 and 10. The mean of all five was 8. What was the fifth score?' (3) 'A new pupil then scored 0 on the spelling test. Does the mean go up, down, or stay the same? Work it out.' (Set the task and WATCH — do not hint at total = mean × count or at what happens with the zero.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Task (1) alone cannot separate rule-following from understanding — both produce 82. Task (2) can only be solved by treating the mean as the total shared equally (total = mean × count); a child with only the add-and-divide rule re-averages the four values or divides by the wrong count. Task (3) directly exposes the well-documented belief that adding a 0 leaves the mean unchanged. The three together separate a child who owns the fair-share meaning from one who has only the procedure.
